title: not a git repository

matcher.pattern: fatal: not a git repository

jokes: This isn't a git repo. It's just a folder with dreams.
There is no .git here. There never was.
fatal: not a git repository (or you're in the wrong folder, again).
This directory has no version control and no memory of its past.
You tried to git something that was never git-ified.

fix.summary: Run git init, or cd into the actual repo.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Not a git repo. cd into the actual project before you start typing commands.
There's no .git here. Wrong directory, wrong day, or both.

title: merge conflict

matcher.pattern: CONFLICT \(content\): Merge conflict in (.+)

jokes: '{file}' has a merge conflict. Two timelines, one file, no peace.
Git found a conflict in '{file}' and refuses to guess which version you meant.
'{file}' is now a battlefield of <<<<<<< and >>>>>>>.
Merge conflict in '{file}': the git equivalent of two people talking over each other.
You and your past self disagree about '{file}'. Sort it out.

fix.summary: Open the file, resolve the conflict markers, then add and continue.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Merge conflict in '{file}'. Pull more often and this stops happening quite so much.
'{file}' has conflicting changes. Resolve them by hand, like every generation before you.

title: detached HEAD

matcher.pattern: You are in 'detached HEAD' state

jokes: You're in detached HEAD state. Your commits are floating in the void, unattached to any branch.
Detached HEAD: you're a commit adrift with no branch to call home.
This is what happens when you checkout a commit hash directly. Bold choice.
You're not on any branch right now. Existentially and literally.
HEAD has detached from reality, or at least from a branch.

fix.summary: Create a branch here if you want to keep this work, or checkout a real branch.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Detached HEAD. You checked out a commit directly again, didn't you.
You're not on a branch. Create one before you commit anything you care about.

title: non-fast-forward push rejected

matcher.pattern: ! \[rejected\].*\(non-fast-forward\)

jokes: The remote has commits you don't. Pull before you push, always.
Push rejected: someone (possibly you, on another machine) got there first.
Non-fast-forward: your local branch and reality have diverged.
Git is protecting the remote from your outdated view of history.
You tried to overwrite history that already moved on without you.

fix.summary: Pull (with rebase if you prefer clean history) before pushing again.

title: nothing to commit, working tree clean

matcher.pattern: nothing to commit, working tree clean

jokes: Nothing to commit. You either finished, or forgot to save your file.
Working tree clean: suspiciously clean, if you were expecting changes.
There's nothing here. Did you actually edit anything?
Git says everything's fine. That's either great news or a sign you forgot to save.
Clean working tree: the calm before you realize you edited the wrong file.

fix.summary: Confirm your edits were saved and are in the expected directory.

sarcastic-senior-dev: Nothing staged. Either you're done, or you forgot to save the file. It's usually the latter.
No changes to commit. Check your editor actually saved before you panic.

title: Permission denied (publickey)

matcher.pattern: Permission denied \(publickey\)

jokes: Your SSH key and GitHub are not on speaking terms.
Permission denied: the remote has never met your public key.
GitHub doesn't recognize you. Have you added your SSH key?
This is what happens when your key is registered on a different machine.
SSH auth failed. Your keyring and your GitHub account need to be introduced.

fix.summary: Check your SSH key is added to the agent and registered with the remote.

title: remote origin already exists

matcher.pattern: fatal: remote (\S+) already exists

jokes: Remote '{remote}' already exists. You already did this step.
You tried to add '{remote}' twice. Git remembers everything.
'{remote}' is already registered. No need to repeat yourself.
This remote is already here. Déjà vu, but for git config.
Adding '{remote}' again won't work — it's already in the family.

fix.summary: Use set-url to change it, or remove it first.

title: file exceeds GitHub's file size limit

matcher.pattern: file is (\d+(?:\.\d+)?\s?\w*B); this exceeds GitHub's file size limit

jokes: That file is {size}. GitHub has limits. You have exceeded them.
You tried to push a {size} file. GitHub said absolutely not.
{size} is too large for a git repo and you know it.
This file belongs in Git LFS, not your regular history.
GitHub rejected your {size} file like a bouncer at a club.

fix.summary: Use Git LFS for large files, or remove it from history.

title: local changes would be overwritten by checkout

matcher.pattern: error: Your local changes to the following files would be overwritten by checkout

jokes: Git refuses to throw away your uncommitted work, unlike you.
Your local changes are in the way. Git is protecting you from yourself.
You have uncommitted changes and git will not silently discard them.
This is git being the responsible adult in the room.
Commit or stash first. Git isn't going to guess what you meant.

fix.summary: Commit or stash your changes before checking out.

title: pathspec did not match any file(s) known to git

matcher.pattern: error: pathspec '([^']+)' did not match any file\(s\) known to git

jokes: '{ref}' doesn't exist. Neither branch nor file. It's a myth.
Git looked for '{ref}' and drew a total blank.
There is no '{ref}' here. Check your spelling, or your assumptions.
'{ref}': not a branch, not a file, not a real thing in this repo.
You referenced something that simply isn't in this repository.

fix.summary: Check the branch/file name for typos, or fetch it first.

title: cannot lock ref

matcher.pattern: fatal: cannot lock ref

jokes: Git's internal state is stuck. A stale lock file is probably the culprit.
Something's holding a ref lock and it won't let go.
Git tried to update a ref and got blocked by leftover lock files.
This is usually a crashed git process leaving junk behind.
The .git directory has some stale housekeeping to do.

fix.summary: Remove the stale lock file in .git/refs, then retry.

title: have diverged

matcher.pattern: have diverged,?\s*$

jokes: Your branch and the remote diverged. Like an old couple, but with commits.
Diverged branches: two different histories claiming to be the truth.
You and origin took different paths. Now git wants you to pick one.
Divergence: git's polite way of saying 'you both have opinions'.
This needs a merge, rebase, or a moment of quiet reflection.

fix.summary: Decide between merge or rebase to reconcile the histories.

title: remote does not appear to be a git repository

matcher.pattern: fatal: '([^']+)' does not appear to be a git repository

jokes: '{remote}' isn't a git repository. Maybe it's a typo, maybe it never existed.
You pushed to '{remote}' and git found nothing resembling a repo there.
'{remote}' does not appear to be a git repository, because it probably isn't one.
Double-check that URL. '{remote}' is not what you think it is.
This is what happens when you paste the wrong remote URL.
Git went looking for a repository at '{remote}' and came back confused.

fix.summary: Check the remote URL is correct and reachable.

title: could not apply commit during rebase

matcher.pattern: error: could not apply (\w+)\.\.\.

jokes: Commit {commit} doesn't apply cleanly. The rebase has hit a wall.
Rebase paused on {commit} because two changes overlap.
{commit} conflicts with what's already been replayed. Resolve and continue.
This is rebase's way of saying 'you two need to talk it out'.
The rebase is stuck on {commit} until you fix the conflict markers.
You're mid-rebase and {commit} refused to land quietly.

fix.summary: Resolve the conflict, git add the files, then continue the rebase.

title: refusing to merge unrelated histories

matcher.pattern: fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories

jokes: These two branches have never met before in their entire commit history.
Git is refusing to pretend these histories were ever the same story.
Unrelated histories: you're trying to merge two repos that don't share an ancestor.
This usually means someone re-initialized a repo somewhere along the way.
Git wants proof these two timelines are actually related. It has none.
You can force it, but git wants you to know these commits are strangers.

fix.summary: Pass --allow-unrelated-histories if you're sure this merge is intentional.

title: git-lfs is not installed

matcher.pattern: git: 'lfs' is not a git command

jokes: This repo wants Git LFS and your machine has never heard of it.
'lfs' is not a git command, because you haven't installed the extension for it.
Somewhere, large binary files are waiting for an LFS client that isn't here.
Git doesn't ship LFS support out of the box. You have to want it.
This repo has LFS pointers and your git has no idea what to do with them.
Install git-lfs, or those 'files' will stay as tiny pointer text forever.

fix.summary: Install Git LFS and run its one-time setup.

title: submodule not initialized

matcher.pattern: fatal: no submodule mapping found in \.gitmodules for path '([^']+)'

jokes: '{path}' is a submodule that was never actually initialized.
That empty folder at '{path}' isn't empty by accident, it's an uninitialized submodule.
Git cloned the pointer to '{path}' but never fetched what it points to.
'{path}' needs its own clone step. Cloning the parent repo wasn't enough.
Submodules don't come along for free on a normal clone.
This is the classic 'forgot --recurse-submodules' story.

fix.summary: Initialize and fetch the submodules.

title: Please tell me who you are

matcher.pattern: Please tell me who you are

jokes: Git has no idea who you are, and it refuses to commit anonymously.
You never configured your name or email, and git just noticed.
This is a brand new machine, or a brand new git config, taking its toll.
Git wants a name and email before it will attribute this commit to anyone.
Every commit needs an author. You haven't told git who that is.
This is the first-commit-on-a-new-machine rite of passage.

fix.summary: Set your git user name and email, locally or globally.
fix.command: git config --global user.email "you@example.com" && git config --global user.name "Your Name"

title: Authentication failed for HTTPS remote

matcher.pattern: fatal: Authentication failed for '([^']+)'

jokes: '{remote}' doesn't recognize your credentials. Or your password stopped working months ago.
GitHub retired password auth for git years ago. You need a token now.
Authentication failed for '{remote}': your username and password combo is not enough anymore.
This is what happens when you type your account password where a token belongs.
'{remote}' wants a personal access token, not the password you've used since 2019.
Your credentials didn't work, and typing them again won't fix that.

fix.summary: Use a personal access token (or SSH) instead of your account password.

title: ambiguous argument: unknown revision or path

matcher.pattern: fatal: ambiguous argument '([^']+)': unknown revision or path not in the working tree

jokes: '{ref}' is not a commit, branch, tag, or file. Git has no idea what you meant.
You referenced '{ref}' and git searched everywhere it knows to look. Nothing.
This is either a typo, an unfetched branch, or a path that was never there.
'{ref}': ambiguous to git, meaningless to your filesystem.
Git needs '--' before path arguments sometimes. This might be one of those times.
'{ref}' doesn't resolve to anything git recognizes right now.

fix.summary: Check the ref exists locally (git fetch if it's remote) or add -- before path arguments.
